profiles.name: Harlow Ballard
profiles.description: Harlow G. Ballard III was an Army captain and physician stationed at Fort Devens, Massachusetts. He refused an order to deploy to Saudi Arabia during the Gulf War and sought conscientious-objector status, explaining that he did not believe any war could be just. Reporting in March 1991 said that he was continuing the discharge process after the fighting ended. No arrest, court-martial or confinement has been documented.
profiles.finding: Deseret News March 22 1991 confirms Fort Devens physician. Doximity Harlow G Ballard III portrait lead requires continuity with 1991 objector; not deployed.
profiles.rights: No image ingested; no public-domain or reuse license inferred.

profiles.name: Jackie Allen-Doucot
profiles.description: Jackie Allen-Doucot was 22 and working as a nursery-school teacher in Hartford when she joined the Griffiss Plowshares action on November 24, 1983. She and six other activists entered Griffiss Air Force Base in Rome, New York, hammered on a B-52 bomber, poured blood, and were arrested. She later joined the Thames River Plowshares action on September 4, 1989, swimming to the USS Pennsylvania at New London, Connecticut. Allen-Doucot has remained active in the Catholic Worker and Plowshares movements.

profiles.name: Gerald Vincent Hoy
profiles.description: Gerald Vincent Hoy was a computer scientist from Easton, Pennsylvania, and a longtime participant in the Irish-American support movement. Federal agents arrested him on July 12, 1989 in the Boston prosecution alleging efforts to provide weapons technology to the Irish Republican Army. Hoy pleaded guilty to related charges and received a two-year federal prison sentence. He was held at FCI Ray Brook and released on June 20, 1992.

profiles.name: Peg Millett
profiles.description:
Peg Millett (Margaret Millett) was an Earth First! activist from Prescott, Arizona and a member of the small EMETIC affinity group. On May 30, 1989 she was surrounded with Mark Davis and Marc Baker in the Arizona desert by some 50 FBI agents in the THERMCON sting; she escaped through the underbrush, hitchhiked back to Prescott, and was arrested the next day at the Planned Parenthood clinic where she worked. She pleaded guilty to attempting to destroy an electrical transmission line used in interstate commerce, was sentenced to 3 years in federal prison, and was ordered to pay $19,821 in restitution.

Earth First! activist arrested in the 1989 EMETIC sting (Evan Mecham Eco-Terrorist International Conspiracy) for conspiracy to sabotage power lines to nuclear facilities in the Southwest. Convicted in federal court in Phoenix and incarcerated under register #32118-008. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

profiles.name: Samuel Sánchez
profiles.description: Samuel Sánchez, a 28-year-old mental-health worker, was held in civil contempt on January 24, 1989 by Judge Eugene Nickerson for refusing to cooperate with a Brooklyn federal grand jury investigating the FALN / Puerto Rican independence movement. He had been subpoenaed days after undergoing skull-reconstruction surgery; FBI agents reportedly tried to interrogate him at his hospital bedside. He refused to inform, telling the court, "I say no to the grand jury."

profiles.name: Marcia Timmel
profiles.description: Marcia Timmel was a longtime member of the Olive Branch / Dorothy Day Catholic Worker in Washington, DC, and one of the most active women in the early Plowshares movement. She participated in Plowshares Number Four (1982) and acted alone in the 1988 Credo Plowshares, where she hammered and poured blood on a Textron Defense System MX missile display at the Air Force Association Arms Bazaar at the Sheraton-Washington Hotel, leaving her own creed of life and faith in response to the bazaar's slogan "Freedom: A Creed To Believe In."

profiles.name: Bob Brown
profiles.description: Bob Brown was an organizer and leader of the All-African People’s Revolutionary Party. A federal grand jury investigating alleged violations of restrictions on travel and financial dealings with Libya ordered Brown, American Indian Movement leaders Vernon Bellecourt and Bill Means, and others to testify. Brown refused to give evidence about political organizations and was found in civil contempt. He entered custody on September 14, 1988, joined a hunger strike that began in the Alexandria Detention Center, and was later transferred to the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York. He served a 90-day contempt sentence.
